analysis.evidence: The next verb, וַיָּבֹאוּ, gives their arrival at En-mishpat (Kadesh). The marked verb describes the preceding change of direction.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine plural, continuing the account of the kings’ movements.

analysis.evidence: וַיָּשֻׁבוּ means “they turned back,” and וַיָּבֹאוּ continues the same group’s movement. The phrase אֶל עֵין מִשְׁפָּט identifies En-mishpat as their destination.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol. The י־ prefix and ־וּ ending mark the third person masculine plural. The subject is Chedorlaomer and the kings with him.

analysis.evidence: In וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל עֵין מִשְׁפָּט, “they came to En-mishpat,” אֶל introduces the place they reached. The following הִוא קָדֵשׁ identifies it as Kadesh.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition without a prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אֶל marks עֵין מִשְׁפָּט as the destination, and הִוא קָדֵשׁ identifies it as Kadesh. The proper-name tag fits the whole name, “Spring of Judgment.” Within that name, עֵין means “spring of.”
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular construct noun. עֵין is the construct form of עַיִן and takes מִשְׁפָּט as its complement.

analysis.evidence: עֵין מִשְׁפָּט means “spring of judgment.” The clause הִוא קָדֵשׁ identifies the whole place-name with Kadesh. Within that name, מִשְׁפָּט supplies the sense “judgment.”
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the absolute state. It completes the construct phrase headed by עֵין.
analysis.sense: judgment: the hearing, the decision, the sentence

analysis.evidence: In עֵין מִשְׁפָּט הִוא קָדֵשׁ, the pronoun links two names for the same place, “En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh.” It serves as the copula in this identification.
analysis.morphology: Independent third-person feminine singular pronoun, written הִוא and read הִיא.
analysis.sense: is (in a clause without a verb)

analysis.evidence: The travelers come to עֵין מִשְׁפָּט (En-mishpat). The phrase הִוא קָדֵשׁ (“that is Kadesh”) gives another name for the same destination.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Kadesh, the place also called En-mishpat

analysis.evidence: The kings return and reach Kadesh. The two אֶת phrases identify the targets of their attack as the whole territory of the Amalekites and the Amorites living at Hazazon-tamar. These direct objects support the military sense of נָכָה.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ introduces a Hiphil wayyiqtol. The י־ prefix and ־וּ ending mark the third person masculine plural.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks כָּל שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי, “all the territory of the Amalekites,” as the definite direct object of וַיַּכּוּ, “they struck.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיַּכּוּ אֶת כָּל שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי, the object of “they struck” is the Amalekite territory. כָּל marks the full extent of that territory.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, governing שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי.

analysis.evidence: In וַיַּכּוּ אֶת כָּל שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי, the attackers strike “all the territory of the Amalekites.” The collective singular הָעֲמָלֵקִי identifies the people whose land is meant.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, with הָעֲמָלֵקִי as its complement.
analysis.sense: territory, the land of a people

draft.change: Add the Hebrew gentilic derived from עֲמָלֵק. The ק belongs to the base name, as Genesis 36:12 shows.
draft.definition: A member of the people of Amalek, or the Amalekites collectively.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:7 uses the singular for the people whose territory was struck. In 2 Samuel 1:8 a man uses the same gentilic to identify himself as an Amalekite.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי, “all the territory of the Amalekites,” שְׂדֵה is in construct and הָעֲמָלֵקִי identifies the people whose territory the kings struck. The following הָאֱמֹרִי, “the Amorites,” likewise designates a people with a singular gentilic.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ precedes a masculine singular absolute gentilic noun. The ending ־ִי forms the gentilic from עֲמָלֵק. The singular refers collectively to the people.

analysis.evidence: The repeated object marker אֶת shows that וְגַם adds the Amorites living at Hazezon-tamar as a second object of וַיַּכּוּ (“they struck”), after the whole territory of the Amalekites.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וְ means “and.” The additive particle גַם means “also” and places the focus on אֶת הָאֱמֹרִי.

analysis.evidence: In וְגַם אֶת הָאֱמֹרִי, וְגַם adds a second object of וַיַּכּוּ (‘they struck’). The marked אֶת introduces הָאֱמֹרִי (‘the Amorites’), which is definite by its article.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:7 as an example of the collective use of the existing amorite sense.
draft.definition: A member of the Amorite people, or collectively the people as a whole.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:7 uses the singular gentilic for the Amorites living at Hazazon-tamar.

analysis.evidence: After וַיַּכּוּ, “they struck,” וְגַם אֶת introduces the Amorites as a further object of the attack. The phrase הַיֹּשֵׁב בְּחַצְצֹן תָּמָר identifies them by where they lived.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ precedes a masculine singular gentilic noun in the absolute state. The noun has collective force, and the participle הַיֹּשֵׁב agrees with it in the singular.
analysis.sense: The Amorite people dwelling at Hazazon-tamar.

analysis.evidence: הַיֹּשֵׁב modifies הָאֱמֹרִי, and בְּחַצְצֹן תָּמָר names the place where the Amorites lived.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes a Qal active participle in the masculine singular absolute. The participle agrees with the collective singular הָאֱמֹרִי.
analysis.sense: to dwell habitually in a place

analysis.evidence: The following תָּמָר completes the place name. Together, בְּחַצְצֹן תָּמָר specifies where the Amorites described by הַיֹּשֵׁב were living.
analysis.morphology: The locative preposition בְּ is prefixed to the first element of the compound place name חַצְצוֹן תָּמָר.

analysis.evidence: הַיֹּשֵׁב בְּחַצְצֹן תָּמָר means “who dwelt in Hazezon-tamar.” The locative בְּ is attached to חַצְצֹן, and תָּמָר completes the name of the place where the Amorites lived.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The marked word is the second component of the place name and has no prefix or suffix.
